item.title: What kind of questions can we ask the I Ching?
item.description:
Quite recently, I saw a post on reddit with a very important question. So much so that I decided to write an article about it with my answer. Here is the original question:

What questions the i ching do not answer ?
#

I am not asking “what is best to ask” (example “ask on how to be a better person”) Also i am not asking “how to phrase the questions so i can get the clearest answer” So not the usual yes/no questions debate (though if someone wants to add about this stuff above , than it is an appreciated bonus , but just as an added thing about the topic , so a good answer can be : " i ching does not answer questions about what is the tastiest food you can get today , and also you should ask i ching for advice and not “yes/no” questions if you want to get a clear answer" )

item.title: How to Use the Liu Yao Method to Find Lost Objects
item.description: Losing objects is one of the most common situations in daily life. It is also deeply stressful becuase it makes us waste time almost always when we least can afford to. While we could certainly perform a classic I Ching consultation to help us find lost objects, and such consultations can give us clues based on the images in the hexagram texts, consulting the I Ching in the classic way is not the most efficient method for finding lost objects. Did you know that there is a divination method based on the I Ching specifically designed for this kind of situation?

item.title: Constrained Stochastic Hermeneutical Computing: A Kinesthetic-Entropy I Ching Protocol
item.description: This white paper outlines Constrained Stochastic Hermeneutical Computing (CSHC), a framework that strips mysticism from the I Ching to deploy it as a finite-state reasoning engine.

item.title: The Mountain and the Innocent Hand: On the Right Attitude Toward the I Ching
item.description: What, according to the I Ching itself, should someone who consults the I Ching seeking wisdom or a deep perspective on a crossroads or complex situation keep in mind?

item.title: Hexagram 1 of this project - Why was El I Chingón born? (About @ElIChingon)
item.description: The project’s origins through personal search, formal languages, and the wisdom of the I Ching.

item.title: I Ching Hexagram 11 and the First Principle of Tai Chi: Body Alchemy to Transform Your Practice
item.description: The first principle of Tai Chi poses the riddle of ’empty intention’. Through I Ching Hexagrams 11 and 12, this article unveils how to invert the usual alignment of the body so that Heaven and Earth meet within you, turning stagnation into dynamic peace and living energy.

item.title: The Numerical Bridge: Bach’s Musical Architecture and the I Ching
item.description: An exploration of how Bach’s numerical signatures mirror the I Ching, revealing a path from disciplined structure to the effortless action of Wu Wei.

item.title: Is there a Connection Between the Peking Opera and the I Ching?
item.description: Analysis of how the principles of the Book of Changes manifest in Peking Opera: vital rhythm, colors, roles, and music.

item.title: What do the I Ching and the Japanese creation myth have in common?
item.description: The connection between Hexagram 1 of the I Ching and the creation myth of the Kojiki is structural and linguistic. The creators of the Japanese myth did not copy the story, but they did adopt the philosophical language and cosmogonic model of the I Ching to narrate their own origins.

item.title: The I Ching and the Universe that Computes Itself
item.description: From antiquity to particle colliders and artificial intelligence, the most fundamental question persists: What is the universe? In this article, we propose a bold synthesis: the universe is not made of solid matter, but of information. The I Ching, with its binary system of Yin and Yang, anticipated this idea long ago. Today, quantum physics shows us that reality, at its most fundamental level, behaves like ‘running software’. But if the universe is code, where does consciousness fit in? Are we mere spectators, or are we the universe processing itself? We explore this paradox through the lens of Eastern philosophy (Tao Te Ching, Buddhism) and the challenges posed by modern science, such as David Chalmers’ ‘Hard Problem of Consciousness’.

item.title: The Symbolism of Holy Week Through the Lens of the I Ching
item.description: We explore how the I Ching encodes the mystery of Christ’s death and resurrection in hexagrams 23 (Disintegration), 2 (The Earth), and 24 (The Return), revealing Holy Saturday as a timeless state and the heart of both processes.

item.title: Is the I Ching the First Meme in History? 🤯
item.description: The I Ching is not just an ancient oracle, but the ancestor of all modern memes. This article explores how the 64 hexagrams align with Richard Dawkins’ theory and behave just like the ‘distracted boyfriend’ or any internet viral. An original take bridging ancient philosophy and 21st‑century digital culture.

item.title: How to Consult the I Ching Using the Coin Toss Method
item.description: A practical guide to consulting the I Ching by tossing three coins. It explains the numerical value of each throw, how the 6 hexagram lines are built, the difference between fixed and moving lines, and how to identify the resulting and derived hexagrams.

item.title: The ABC of the I Ching
item.description: The I Ching is more than an oracle: it’s a universal language based on Yin and Yang. This article guides you through its binary alphabet, the 8 trigrams, and the 64 hexagrams, explaining how its words and sentences are structured.

item.title: Chance, Science, and the I Ching: A Convergence in Understanding Order and Uncertainty
item.description: Is chance a tool for knowledge? This article connects the I Ching with quantum mechanics, chaos theory, Gödel’s theorems and bootstrapping to show how chance, far from being an obstacle, rather filters our subjectivity and allows us to access deeper orders.
